units.translation: They row around the head with their hands, escorting
the twisting of the hand, when it is brought down rapidly
the continuous gathering of the hands, rapidly brought down in a crowd
by the din of battle and the shouting
from the dark heartwood of the pine
Βασιλείου τιά-ρας φάλαρον [the cheek-piece of the royal tiara]
Ὦ χαῖρε λαμπτὴρ νυκτὸς ἡμερήσιον φάος [Hail, torch of the night, light of the day]
[Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἐκ γῆς δυσ-φρόνων μειλίγματα βροτοῖς [For the offerings from the earth to the hostile-minded mortals]
Aeschylus used this verb following the example of the epic poets; Sophocles and Euripides never used it.
I bid the eye of my father to follow
the cheek-piece of the royal tiara
Hail, torch of the night, light of the day
For the offerings from the earth to the hostile-minded mortals
about which passage I have spoken under δίπλαξ.
It is constructed with the genitive in the sense of wandering from or being deprived of
Πατροφόνῳ χερὶ τῶν κρεισσοτέκνων ὀμμάτων [by the father-slaying hand of the eyes of the stronger children]
thus Blomfield for δ᾽ ἀπ᾿ ὀμμάτων [but from the eyes]
by the father-slaying hand of the eyes of the stronger children
longoa. A poetic verb used for πελάζω [to approach], whose active present form Sophocles and Euripides used, and the passive aorist form, with intransitive meaning, the same poets and once Aeschylus

that πλασθείην [I might approach] is written in many copies with the same error by which scribes corrupted the adjective of the same root ἄπλατος [unapproachable] usually into ἄπλαστος. To this verb is undoubtedly to be referred what is read
Πόντιαι τ᾽ ἀγκάλαι κνωδάλων ἀνταίων βροτοῖσι [and the sea's arms of hostile sea-monsters to mortals]

which Hermann, in accordance with the antistrophic verses, corrected thus: κνωδάλων ἀνταίων | βρύουσι . πλάθουσι καὶ [of hostile sea-monsters they teem, and they approach] etc. For what some have thought, that πλάθουσι [they approach] is used for πλήθουσι [they are full], as Hesychius explained πλάθους [of approach] by πληθους [of fullness], introduces a Doricism foreign to the tragedians.
I might approach as a husband to one from heaven
they approach; they sprout, and the torches of the earth, raised high
and the sea's arms of hostile sea-monsters to mortals
of hostile sea-monsters they teem, and they approach
Ἀλλά με τὰν τάλαιναν [But me, the wretched one]
Ταὐτά τοι [the same things, you know]
Ὅποι γῆς ἡ μογερὰ [where on earth the toiling one]
Πλανᾷ, κακὸς δὲ ἰατρὸς ὡς τις ἐς νόσον πεσὼν [she wanders, and like a bad doctor who has fallen into illness]
she wanders, fasting, along the sandy shore
wandering, one calamity after another settles upon her
where on earth the toiling one
she wanders, and like a bad doctor who has fallen into illness
Of a wandering and roaming journey
Ποῖ μ᾿ ἄγουσι τηλέπλανοι [Where are the far-wandering ones leading me?]
Thus from the copies for πλάνοι [wanderers].
Ἄδην με πολύπλανοι [the much-wandering ones have had enough of me]
